State Receptiveness to 3rd Party Candidates

Bobby Innes-Gold, The Brookings Institution

As favorability ratings for the Democratic and Republican parties continue to decline, Americans' appetite for a third political alternative is growing. Yet while most Americans express a desire for a competitive third party, few prospective voters actually back one at the ballot box. Historically, American electoral support for third parties has fluctuated across regions and eras. This report analyzes state-level disparities across several key metrics.

I.

Presidential Vote Share

10 presidential elections · 1988–2024

In the past ten presidential elections, some states have been more receptive to third party presidential candidates than others. Three states – Utah, Alaska, and Vermont – have been particularly receptive, each averaging about eight to nine percent of the popular vote since 1988.

II.

Independent Identifiers

Share of each state's electorate identifying as pure independents · surveys 2006–2024

Party identification is a critical factor in shaping how Americans vote. Not surprisingly, people who identify as Democrats vote overwhelmingly for Democratic presidential candidates. Similarly, Americans who identify as Republican overwhelmingly support Republican candidates. Along these lines, research has shown that voters who identify as pure independents – they do not lean in either partisan direction – are more likely to support third-party or independent candidates. Figure 2 examines the proportion of each state’s electorate that identifies as “pure independents” in surveys from 2006 to 2024. Ten states report a percentage of independent identifiers approaching 20 percent or higher. They are Alaska, Arkansas, Connecticut, Hawaii, Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island, Vermont, and West Virginia. Interestingly, five of these ten states have elected third-party candidates to statewide office (Governor or Senator): Alaska, Connecticut, Maine, Rhode Island and Vermont. Minnesota has also done so.

III.

Competitive Elections

Elections in which the third-party share exceeded the Democratic–Republican margin · 1988–2024

In some elections, the margin between the major party candidates is so narrow that the percentage of the vote received by third party candidates exceeds that margin. In a context such as this one, third party candidates are positioned to be very influential. Over the past ten elections, seven states have repeatedly (four times or more) produced scenarios in which the third-party share of the popular vote was greater than the difference between the two major party candidates. These states are Arizona, Florida, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, North Carolina, and Wisconsin. At the same time, in a very competitive election, voters may be less willing to cast a ballot for a third-party candidate who has no chance of winning because they do not want to increase the chances that their least preferred candidate will win.

IV.

Getting onto the Ballot

Petition signatures required of independent presidential candidates · 2024

One of the most significant obstacles facing third party candidates is getting onto the ballot, a process that demands considerable time and resources. Those demands vary widely from state to state. Figure 4 examines the number of petition signatures per thousand eligible voters required for independent candidates in each state for the 2024 presidential election. Some states are very onerous in their signature requirements (Oklahoma, North Carolina); others are extremely lenient (Tennessee, New Jersey). Deadlines for getting onto the ballot also vary by state and impact the signature collection effort.

V.

Voter Registration Rules

Deadline to register to vote in the 2024 general election, by days before Election Day

Research has demonstrated that young people and those less interested in politics are more likely to support a third-party candidate. They are also more likely to register to vote at the last minute. In 1998, former professional wrestler Jesse Ventura, a third-party candidate for the governorship of Minnesota, was propelled to victory largely on the strength of young men who registered on election day and who overwhelmingly supported him. Figure 5 examines registration deadlines across states. States with same-day voter registration (there are 21 of them) provide an opportunity for third-party candidates to attract unlikely voters who may be mobilized very late in the campaign cycle.
